column1: # THE LABEL OWNERSHIP DECLARATION. Machine-readable on purpose.
# Prose cannot stop the failure this exists for: an agent reads the repo, sees
# a label it thinks should be set, and writes automation that sets it -- while
# a different automation, equally reasonably, withdraws it. Neither is wrong
# about the world. The label has no owner. On PR #9 production:healthy flipped
# five times in twenty minutes between a person and github-actions.
# Before adding ANY label write to ANY script or workflow, find its row here.
# If the writer you are adding is not the declared owner, you are building the
# thrash. gates/label-audit.py enforces this against a PR's timeline.
# owner        the ONE thing that may write this label
# human_add    may a person add it by hand?
# human_rm     may a person remove it by hand?
# persistent   does it survive settlement? PERSISTENT labels describe what the
#              change IS and stay true after it ships. TRANSIENT labels mark where
#              a change sat in the deployment process; once it is merged back to
#              main that position adds no value, so settle.sh clears them. The PR
#              timeline keeps the history either way.

column1: # EXCLUSION GROUPS. Cardinality is a different fact from ownership.
# SPLIT 2026-09-13: classification moved to itil:* and change:* now holds only
# the lifecycle. The two were mixed in one namespace, which is why the rule
# "a PR has at most one change:*" could not be stated -- change:standard plus
# change:complete was a legitimate pair and occurred six times. itil:* names
# the ITIL change type; change:* names where the change record has got to.
# The rows above say who may WRITE each label. They cannot say that two labels
# are mutually exclusive, and that turned out to matter: #2 carried
# change:standard AND change:emergency at once, which left its class undefined
# while every rule in preflight branches on the class.
# Note the rule is NOT "at most one change:*". change:standard + change:complete
# is a legitimate pair and occurs six times in this repo's history. The change:*
# namespace holds TWO kinds of fact and the exclusion applies within each:
#   class      what kind of change this is       exactly one, once classified
#   lifecycle  where it is in the process        at most one ACTIVE state
# That overloading is a naming defect, recorded rather than renamed: renaming
# change:standard now would rewrite the class of every settled change in the
# history, and the history is the record.

column6: TERMINAL. ITIL closure code: the change did not complete. Production never served it, or never had it made live. Nothing to undo
TERMINAL. ITIL closure code: production DID serve this change and was returned to a prior state. abort.sh refuses this without --to <sha>, because the word asserts an estate action

AN UNPAID CHANGE RECORD. An emergency lands first and is documented after -- ITIL documents an emergency change retrospectively, and blocking on the record would make the record the emergency. This label says a change reached main without the normal evidence and still owes: the window it never booked, the observations it never took, and why. It blocks NOTHING. A person adds it when declaring an emergency and a person clears it when the record is written; automation must not clear a debt it did not pay. PERSISTENT: it must survive settlement, because the merge is when the debt STARTS -- a label that vanished at settle would clear itself at the exact moment the change went in undocumented

INTENT. The one thing a person must say. Supersedes change:requested + release, which were two human-owned labels for one fact. An external change-request reference, if any, belongs in the change record and not in the label

The staging lease outlived its holder -- berth held, window gone, build serving nowhere. Found live on #92, where the intent was long dead and the lock was not. Written by the reaper; a person may clear it after coordinating. Nothing else names this state, and it blocks everyone via guard 1

A recorded proxy approval. NEVER equals APPROVED: guard4.sh prints which it found so nobody reads one as the other, and it requires an observation record naming the reviewed SHA -- a label cannot say which build was read
